question: The pressure \(P\) of wind on a sail varies jointly as the area \(A\) of the sail and the square of the velocity \(V\) of the wind. The pressure on a square foot is \(1\) pound when the velocity is \(16\) miles per hour. The velocity of the wind when the pressure on a square yard is \(36\) pounds is:
solution:
First express both pressures for the same sail area. A square yard measures \(3\) feet by \(3\) feet, so it contains \(9\) square feet. Thus \(36\) pounds on a square yard is
\[
\frac{36}{9}=4
\]
pounds per square foot.

The stated joint variation means that pressure per unit area is proportional to the square of wind speed. The pressure per square foot has increased from \(1\) pound to \(4\) pounds, so, if the new speed is \(V\),
\[
\left(\frac{V}{16}\right)^2=4.
\]
Wind speed is nonnegative, and the positive pressure rules out zero. Therefore \(V/16=2\), giving \(V=32\) mph. The answer is \(\boxed{32\text{ mph}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
